summary_responses.response: Modern cloud services, built on microservice architectures, often suffer from temporary overloads that cause valuable user transactions to be rejected. Existing retry mechanisms can worsen these situations by creating "retry storms" that don't distinguish between high and low-priority requests. The paper proposes a simple, distributed mechanism called DiffTry (Differential Retries), which assigns more retry attempts to high-priority requests and fewer to low-priority ones. This approach effectively prioritizes important transactions during overload periods without requiring complex coordination or overload detection. The authors provide a mathematical model to predict DiffTry's performance and validate its effectiveness through simulations and a live deployment on a Kubernetes network, showing it significantly reduces rejections for high-value traffic.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is issuing a new airworthiness directive for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. The directive was prompted by reports of low clearance between fuel lines, hydraulic systems, and other components within the right wing. This unsafe condition could create an ignition source in the fuel tank if the aircraft is struck by lightning. The new rule requires inspections and corrective actions to rectify the clearance issues. This final rule will become effective on November 18, 2026, and is estimated to affect 60 airplanes in the U.S.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to update its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations for federal employees. This rule incorporates recent statutory amendments that broaden the types of service qualifying for FMLA eligibility. Specifically, almost all federal civilian service, including temporary or intermittent work, and certain honorable active military service will now count toward the required 12 months of service. The changes also clarify that annual and sick leave earned under systems outside of the standard title 5 authority can be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave. Finally, the rule formally excludes certain Veterans Health Administration employees from title 5 FMLA coverage, as they are now covered under a separate authority.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Office of Personnel Management is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate statutory amendments from January 2021 and December 2023.
The rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026.
The statutory changes make virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility.
The rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage.

The December 2023 amendment allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility, but does not include service in the Coast Guard or commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.
The minimum qualifying service for FMLA eligibility under title 5 is 12 months.
